stories.headline: Democrats Gain Ground in North Carolina Senate Race as Polls Face Scrutiny
stories.summary:
Democrats appear to have momentum in North Carolina, particularly in the Senate race. Former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, faces Republican political operative Michael Whatley for the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). The Hill reported that polling, nonpartisan ratings and campaign shifts suggest Cooper is poised to win.

The report noted that a national Republican PAC has been involved in the race. A veteran Democratic strategist who managed Barack Obama's narrow 2008 victory in the state urged donors and supporters to stay focused on Cooper's campaign rather than assume the outcome is settled.

The race is one of several that will help determine control of the Senate. The Cook Political Report recently shifted 18 races toward Democrats and projected a net gain of 9 to 19 House seats. Right-leaning outlets have urged caution. The Washington Examiner reported that polls showing Democrats leading in the midterms are coming under scrutiny, a reminder that public polling has been criticized in past cycles. Republicans have also been pulling ads from races they see as unwinnable, a sign of electoral anxiety. The midterm elections are weeks away.

stories.headline: Fugitive Businessman Alvaro Pulido Taken Into US Custody in Venezuela Bribery Case
stories.summary:
Alvaro Pulido, a businessman wanted for years in the United States, has been taken into custody. He is accused of paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela, according to an Associated Press report carried by the Washington Examiner and CBS News.

Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted President Nicolas Maduro. The Drug Enforcement Administration and the State Department had offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.

The arrest comes as the US legal case against Maduro and his circle continues. Maduro and his wife have recently been charged with conspiracy to commit torture, and a co-defendant was added to a narco-terrorism count. The report did not say where Pulido was arrested or when he will appear in court.

stories.headline: Update: Poland Detains Man Suspected of Plotting to Assassinate Prime Minister Tusk
stories.summary:
Polish police have detained a man accused of plotting an assassination attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. The suspect, identified as Polish national Jacek Dobrzynski, was arrested in the Lower Silesia region. Tusk thanked police for their "swift and decisive action."

The plot came to light when an email describing the potential attack was forwarded to police by the State Protection Service, which handles ministers' security. Security services convened a special meeting on Sunday, and a spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious." He added that there was "a strong likelihood that these threats could actually be carried out."

The arrest is a new development beyond earlier reporting that security services were probing a threat to Tusk. It comes amid heightened security concern in Poland after a series of school stabbings that Tusk has said were driven by online glorification of violence. Tusk, prime minister since 2023 after an earlier term from 2007 to 2014, also served as president of the European Council. Authorities have not yet said what the suspect's motive was or what charges he will face.

stories.headline: Trump's Late Midterm Deals Draw Backlash Within GOP, as Mullin Briefs on Hurricane Isaias
stories.summary:
On CBS's Face the Nation, host Margaret Brennan framed the week around President Trump's last-minute deals ahead of the midterms, 23 days away, and the resulting backlash within his own party. The latest was the deal with Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to lower fuel prices. Senate Republican whip John Barrasso was scheduled to be asked whether the deal will prompt more GOP candidates to distance themselves from Trump.

Democrats also face challenges, notably turning out their own loyalists. Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut and New Hampshire Senate nominee Rep. Chris Pappas were scheduled to discuss the party's strategy. Trump has been campaigning for loyalists in states such as Tennessee, saying of the effort, "What the hell am I doing in Tennessee?"

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also gave an update on Hurricane Isaias, the first Atlantic hurricane of the year, which made landfall Friday night and killed four people. Hundreds of thousands lost power. Mullin said federal officials were in touch with affected governors, that FEMA assets had been prepositioned, and that governors reported being in good shape. The program also covered ICE tactics after a shooting in New York City, and an interview on AI with Palantir's chief technology officer.

stories.headline: Czech Premier Babis's ANO Party Weakens in Regional Elections
stories.summary:
Support for ANO, the party of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, weakened in regional elections held across the Czech Republic. The losses came mainly in larger cities, according to Bloomberg.

The vote is a test of the governing party's standing. Regional results can signal shifts in national political sentiment, though the pool offered limited detail on final tallies or which parties gained.

Further results and analysis of the coalition implications are expected as counting concludes.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Announces Russia-Ukraine 'Energy Ceasefire' as Zelensky Says Kyiv Would Agree if Moscow Does
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced on Sunday on Truth Social that "effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," saying both parties had agreed. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios the announcement "was news for me," but said Ukraine would agree if Russia does. It remains unclear whether Moscow has accepted. The Kremlin had said earlier that there would be no immediate resumption of talks to end the war.

The announcement followed a day of escalating friction between Washington and Kyiv. Trump had demanded that Zelensky halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blamed him for high U.S. diesel prices, and suggested Ukraine needs "a new leader." This came after the administration's deal to buy Russian diesel and waive some sanctions. Zelensky, speaking on ABC's "This Week," called the deal a "birthday gift" to Vladimir Putin that gives him money to "kill us, kill our children." He said the next Ukrainian leader would be chosen by the Ukrainian people, and that elections could be held if Putin agrees to a two-month ceasefire. Ukraine has pushed for a 60-day full ceasefire.

The diesel deal has drawn criticism from some Republicans. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) said he would introduce a bipartisan bill, the "Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act," and force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said the sanctions easing may be breaking the law, and Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) backed lowering diesel prices but opposed importing from Putin. The administration has presented the deal as a way to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, with truckers reporting diesel at $6.32 per gallon. Analysts say the fuel would take weeks to ship and the quantities are too small to affect prices much. The European Commission's Ursula von der Leyen voiced full support for Zelensky.

stories.headline: Poland Says School Stabbings Driven by Online Glorification of Violence; Security Services Probe Threat to Tusk
stories.summary:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the online "glorification of violence." Speaking after a crisis meeting with security services on Sunday, he said the attacks were "very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity" and that authorities were not dealing with any large organized group. One woman has been killed and others, including children, were injured.

The attacks began Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student injured nine people at a vocational school in Mazovia. On Thursday a 15-year-old killed a 37-year-old caretaker at a primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny. On Saturday a woman injured three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in Warsaw. Thousands of police officers visited schools nationwide Friday to reassure pupils after rumors spread of a "Bloody Friday" tied to a supposed online challenge, and 117 people have been arrested for carrying knives or other weapons or for threatening attacks.

Tusk described the violence as "nihilistic" and associated with the extreme right, saying some detainees are active in ultra-right circles and that police noted a rise in online searches for Nazi content and for mass killers who have become online idols. Separately, Polish security services held a special meeting after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, which a spokesperson said was being treated as "deadly serious." A man allegedly plotting an assassination attempt on Tusk has been detained.

stories.headline: Fresh Floods Sweep Away Homes and Bridges in Nepal's Gorkha District
stories.summary:
A major river in Nepal's central Gorkha district flooded on Sunday, sweeping away about a dozen houses and several suspension bridges and damaging a hydropower station, authorities said. The army rescued around 50 people from the banks of the Budhi Gandaki River. No deaths have been reported, but five people are missing.

Water levels at one location rose from two metres to nearly 8.5 metres within a couple of hours, and a hydrological station was swept away, cutting off data. The cause is unclear: some suggest a landslide dammed the river or a tributary before bursting, while others cite an ice avalanche upstream. Experts say the debris flow was much smaller and slower than the August flash floods.

The flood struck as families prepared to mark the first day of the Dashain festival. Nepal is still recovering from catastrophic floods two months ago on its border with Tibet, which left more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing. Save the Children is mobilising an emergency team, with its Nepal director saying children's lives have been "ripped apart in an instant yet again." Many families have been displaced and face uncertainty over shelter and supplies.

stories.headline: El Sayed Blames 'Younger,' 'Angry' Self for Past Obama Criticism Ahead of Joint Michigan Rally
stories.summary:
Abdul el Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that his past criticism of Barack Obama reflected his "younger" and "angry" self. He was asked about reservations over a rally with the former president at the end of the month, given his earlier scrutiny of Obama's foreign, immigration and healthcare policies.

The criticism came in a 2012 Huffington Post op-ed in which el Sayed wrote that Obama had not delivered a promised progressive agenda and "was not the right choice -- he just wasn't the wrong one." On Sunday he said he related to Obama's description of himself in his memoir as someone frustrated and wanting things to be better, adding that "where we push differently, it is because we've learned from what he's done and because we stand on the shoulders of giants."

Obama, speaking at a fundraiser Wednesday, rejected the idea that el Sayed is too far left, citing his support for a higher minimum wage and healthcare for all and saying, "it doesn't seem crazy to me. You know, FDR was for that, too." Polling shows a close race against Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers, and Republicans are directing hundreds of millions in outside spending to defend their narrow Senate majority. Democrats see Obama's involvement as a sign they believe they can flip the seat.

stories.headline: Children Among 109 Dead After Migrant Boat Capsizes Off Djibouti, UN Says
stories.summary:
At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died and dozens more remain missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration said. The vessel was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen with about 350 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 80 people were rescued.

The IOM said the recovered bodies included 52 men, 42 women, nine girls and six boys. The survivors are all Ethiopian nationals, and the agency is assisting 64 of them at its response center in Obock with healthcare and help restoring contact with relatives. IOM Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face, and local authorities are arranging burials.

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa attempt the crossing of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait each year, seeking safety and work in Gulf countries, despite Yemen's decade-long civil war. The IOM said more than 900 migrants died or went missing on the same route in 2025, with attempts rising 18%. A similar incident in March 2026 killed nine and left 45 missing, and the agency has recorded more than 20,000 movements from Ethiopia to Djibouti since 10 September.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV to Undergo Surgery After Lung Nodule Found
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV announced during his Sunday Angelus prayers in St Peter's Square that he will undergo surgery in the coming days after doctors found a nodule on his lung during a medical check-up. The 71-year-old pontiff described it as "early" and "well-localised," and said his medical team believed it right to intervene.

The Holy See Press Office said the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, with about a week of recovery expected. The Pope confirmed that his planned November visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru will still go ahead. A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue usually detected by X-ray or CT scan, and most cause no other symptoms.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, President Sergio Mattarella and Israeli President Isaac Herzog all wished him a swift recovery. Leo, the first US-born pope, succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also suffered lung problems requiring hospital treatment. He has recently drawn public attention for a rift with President Donald Trump, to whom he has responded by saying his mission is to preach peace.

stories.headline: Philadelphia Police Officers Shot 15 Times Combined in Early Morning Ambush
stories.summary:
Two Philadelphia police officers were hospitalized after being shot early Saturday while responding to a report of a man with a gun on a porch in the western part of the city. Commissioner Kevin Bethel said a 40-year-old officer with two children was shot three times, and a 33-year-old officer with five children was shot 12 times. Both were taken to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center for surgery, and their conditions were not immediately clear.

The officers were dispatched to 140 North 52nd Street just after 12:20 a.m. and came under "significant gunfire" on the porch. Additional officers and a SWAT team found them wounded. The suspect fired at two more officers before SWAT located him hiding in a tree and took him into custody.

The suspect, whose name has not been released, was found with two handguns and a shotgun, one of the handguns belonging to a wounded officer. Bethel said, "We are praying now that our officers make it through this terrible situation," and praised the department's officers for consistently going into danger. Fox News and The Hill reported the incident.

stories.headline: Justice Department Opens Antitrust Probe of TV Networks Over Suspended Trump Pool Coverage
stories.summary:
The U.S. Justice Department said it is investigating ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News over whether they violated federal competition law when they suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump last month. The Antitrust Division asked the networks to hand over communications related to the pool and said the boycott could violate the Sherman Act, which bars monopolistic business practices. A department spokesperson said the division is "simply investigating to determine whether these news organisations have violated the antitrust laws." The networks have not yet commented.

The five networks paused their presidential coverage for several days after the administration withdrew the credentials of reporters from CNN, MS Now and Politico. Trump had blocked the three outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his team. Access was later restored after a judge ruled in a lawsuit in which the outlets argued the restrictions violated their First Amendment rights. Pool members normally share their material with the wider media.

The administration has taken a series of actions affecting press access. In February the White House took control of the press pool, which the White House Correspondents' Association had managed for more than a century. The administration also moved to bar Associated Press journalists from limited-access spaces over the outlet's use of "Gulf of Mexico" rather than "Gulf of America"; that lawsuit remains ongoing.

The administration has framed its actions as enforcement of the law, while press-freedom advocates and the outlets argue that government discrimination against coverage it dislikes is barred by the First Amendment. It is unclear what the networks will provide or whether the department will take further action.

stories.headline: Update: Tennessee Inmate Christa Pike Discharged From Hospital 10 Days After Failed Execution
stories.summary:
Christa Pike, the Tennessee death row inmate who survived two lethal injections on September 30, has been discharged from the hospital and returned to the prison where she has been held for 30 years, her lawyers said Saturday. The 50-year-old is continuing to receive medical care. She is believed to be the only person to have survived a lethal injection execution attempt.

Pike regained consciousness earlier this week after her legal team had believed for days that she was brain dead. Her first words, according to lawyer Randy Spivey, were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?" Her lawyers said she was suffering from pneumonia and significant swelling in her arms and could not swallow, and that she felt "angry and confused." They said she was grateful to first responders and her medical team.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said why the execution failed, though it has defended its method, which used pentobarbital. At a hearing Wednesday, an assistant attorney general said he did not know whether the state would try to execute her again. The judge ordered the state to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections, which could support a future lawsuit.

Pike was convicted of the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, committed when Pike was 18. Her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was a minor. The U.S. Supreme Court and Governor Bill Lee had declined to block the execution, and her lawyers are now seeking commutation to life without parole.

stories.headline: Pakistan Imposes State of Emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Stronghold of Imran Khan's Party
stories.summary:
Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday imposed a state of emergency in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, citing "the rising incidents of terrorism and a deteriorating law and order situation." The move came on the recommendation of the federal cabinet.

The prime minister's office said the decision followed the provincial government's "deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism." The province is governed by the party of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, which sets up a direct confrontation between the federal government and the opposition-run provincial administration.

The federal government presents the step as a security measure necessary to counter militant violence. Critics are likely to view it as an attempt to curb the political power of Khan's party in its stronghold, though details of the emergency's scope and any reaction from the provincial government were not immediately available. Further developments are expected as the provincial leadership responds.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Weighs Joining Saudi Strikes on Houthis After Riyadh Airport Attack Kills 12
stories.summary:
Saudi authorities said 12 people were killed and 309 injured in the Saturday strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia since May 2015. The dead included four Saudis and nationals of Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Sudan, the Palestinian territories and the United States. Some of the injured were in critical condition, and the airport temporarily suspended operations.

President Trump denounced the attack as "terrible" and said the United States is evaluating whether to join Saudi Arabia's offensive against the Houthis. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington "strongly condemns" the attacks by the "terrorist Houthis." Saudi-backed forces said 1,150 Houthis were killed in operations over the past 24 hours, a claim not independently verified.

The strike was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab country since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February, and Washington is debating both striking the Houthis and restarting strikes on Iran. Medical services in Taiz, Yemen, are at risk of shutting down under a Houthi blockade. The new development is Trump's statement that the U.S. may join the offensive.
